name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan’s Republican House, Democratic Senate put new fiscal year K-12 funding bills in play
description: Competing visions for Michigan’s 2026-27 K-12 school aid budget were officially in the mix on Tuesday following appropriations panel hearings before the Republican-controlled House of Representatives and the Democratic-led Senate. Both chambers of the Michigan Legislature have been pumping out appropriations bills, a good sign for those watching the budget p[...]
text:
Michigan State Capitol Building | Photo by Jon KingCompeting visions for Michigan’s 2026-27 K-12 school aid budget were officially in the mix on Tuesday following appropriations panel hearings before the Republican-controlled House of Representatives and the Democratic-led Senate.
Both chambers of the Michigan Legislature have been pumping out appropriations bills, a good sign for those watching the budget process closely. The previous budget battle ended late into the year and well after Michigan’s constitutional deadline to have a budget in play for the coming fiscal year. The stalemate ended only after a brief government shutdown and with several concessions from Senate Democrats.
With a costly set of elections at hand in 2026 and seemingly zero will on either side to seriously rock the boat, the budget cycle this year seems to be moving on a swifter, smoother track.
One area of disagreement that might arise is how to fund free meals for students, although both sides did not gut school meals in such a way to cause any major alarm bells.
 Members of the House Appropriations School Aid and Department of Education Subcommittee on Tuesday morning reported an amended school aid budget bill sponsored by the subcommittee’s chair, state Rep. Tim Kelly (R-Saginaw Township).SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX
Later in the afternoon, the Senate Appropriations PreK-12 Subcommittee moved an amended version of its K-12 budget, Senate Bill 858, sponsored by subcommittee chair Sen. Darrin Camilleri (D-Trenton), to its respective full appropriations committee.
Kelly’s House Bill 5628 would fund statewide K-12 programs at $21.52 billion with $67.3 million from the state’s general fund. That amounts to a nearly $236 million increase in funding over the current fiscal year, up 1.1%.
Testimony from Tuesday morning’s committee detailed the House bill increasing state restricted funding by $243 million and reducing federal funding by $2 million. At least $5.8 million in general fund dollars were cut from the proposed House K-12 budget bill, an 8% decrease, but the plan does amount to a 1.1% overall increase from current fiscal year funding.
A 2.5% increase in per-pupil funding is another hallmark of Kelly’s plan, increasing the allowance from $10,050 to $10,300 per student. The estimated cost of total per-pupil funding amounts to $323 million.
Kelly’s budget outlook also increases per-pupil funding for intermediate school districts and the Great Start Readiness Program by 2.5% each.
Nearly $300 million would be appropriated for new curriculum development for districts, including $150 million for literacy support, $100 million for new math curriculum, and $50 million for STEM curriculum.
The House budget has $150 million for “high-impact” tutoring and a $40 million pilot program for districts to reimburse parents for the cost of private tutoring.
State Rep. Tim Kelly (R-Saginaw Township), chair of the House Appropriations School Aid and Department of Education Subcommittee, listens to testimony from Glenn Maleyko, Michigan’s new state superintendent for public instruction. Feb. 3, 2026 | Screenshot
The school aid budget’s rainy day fund would also see a $239.1 million deposit under Kelly’s plan, and a $20 million deposit into a newly created special education reserve fund. The bill would further place $321 million toward mental health and school safety initiatives.
In contrast, the Senate is proposing $22.01 billion for K-12 schools in the next fiscal year, with $50.8 million in from the state general fund, which amounts to a 3.4% increase over the current fiscal year appropriation of $21.2 billion. That also amounts to a 30.5% decrease in general fund dollars toward public schools over the current fiscal year’s $73.1 million level, which was set in October 2025.
Senators included more than $1.5 billion for at-risk students, $300 million for mental health and school safety, $150 million for teacher bonuses, and another $150 million for transportation costs and increased energy demands.
The Senate bill further makes a commitment to literacy enhancements with $235 million-plus for literacy support.
The Senate would seek a new weighted formula as outlined in Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s recommendations. The House version does not adopt Whitmer’s call for a new weighted formula.
The Democratic-led Senate version of the K-12 funding bill aligns with the GOP-led House public schools funding model in that the per-pupil allowance would also be funded at $10,300.
On the free school meals front, the House, Senate and Whitmer’s office agree that they should still be funded at around the same levels, but the approaches vary.
Whitmer’s recommendation cuts out $1.6 million in one-time general fund dollars in lieu of $200 million ongoing school aid fund dollars to fund the program. Whitmer proposed removing non-public schools students from eligibility, however. A requirement would be added under the governor’s proposal for each school district to participate in the National School Breakfast Program.
The House generally agreed, including with Whitmer’s request for participation in the national program, but the chamber revised the $1.6 million one-time general fund cut so that it was baked back into the mix. Its iteration would fund school meals at a total of $201.6 million. The House bill maintains free school meal funding for non-public school students. 
The Senate plan also agreed with Whitmer’s recommendations, but included $1.2 billion to continue the state’s free breakfast and lunch program for non-public school students.
Cross-chamber mudslinging in shorter supply compared to 2025 cycle
Kelly told his committee on Tuesday morning that he did not include a weighted formula because he surmised it was something the parties would get to in the negotiating process.
“We also, I think, have some opportunities for points of differences that we know that we can have for negotiations,” he said.
State Rep. Carol Glanville (D-Walker) asked how the private tutoring would appear in boilerplate language for a final bill, and wondered if it would be an open checkbook for families to spend money on their child’s particular needs.
Kelly said that Michigan, as a state that is nearly last in the nation when grading literacy, needed to do something outside of the box.
“This is one of them,” Kelly said. “There was an opportunity a few years ago to do similar things where the governor vetoed it. We’re going to give it another shot. And I think that there’s ample opportunity for others to help with children and families outside of the traditional role.”
Kelly added that the budget, at least, puts the House’s horse on the track as they begin to negotiate.
Following his subcommittee’s movement on the Senate K-12 budget, Camilleri said that their version “was informed by parents and educators and people who understand one simple truth: there’s no greater investment than the one we make in our children’s future.”
State Sens. Dayna Polehanki (D-Livonia) and Darrin Camilleri (D-Trenton) listen to colleagues during an appropriations subcommittee hearing in which the Senate planned to move forward its 2026-27 Fiscal Year K-12 spending plan. April 21, 2026 | Photo By Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
State Sen. Dayna Polehanki (D-Livonia), who chairs the Senate Education Committee and is a former educator, said boosted reading scores don’t happen overnight, and that it will take long-term investments like the ones the Senate planned to make to right the ship.
“Instead of cutting corners and chasing short-sighted fixes, we’re making consistent, evidence-based investments that give our educators the support they need to help students achieve literacy,” she said.
In a scrum with reporters following the hearing, Camilleri said it is his hope to get the budget done as quickly as they can, which would be an improvement over last year.
Whether he was confident about getting the budget done on time this year, Camilleri said, “we’ll see.”
“That’s always been our mantra out of the state Senate. Let’s be responsible partners and responsible legislators,” he said. “Let’s get this thing done and follow the law and get it done on time. This is better in terms of seeing how they are, finally realizing that they should not be holding up funding for our communities. … I hope that they come to the table and get this thing done as quickly as we can.”

title: NC lawmakers, advocates push Leandro funding as 2026 legislative session opens in Raleigh
description: With courts no longer enforcing the Leandro plan, Rep. Julie von Haefen (D-Wake) on Tuesday renewed her long-running push to fund it in the legislature, as dozens of public school advocates rallied outside the North Carolina General Assembly. This marks the seventh time von Haefen has filed the proposal, which has repeatedly failed to receive […]
text:
Student advocate Morgan Taylor speaks to a crowd in front of the NC Legislative Building on April 21, 2026. (Photo: Ahmed Jallow/NC Newsline) With courts no longer enforcing the Leandro plan, Rep. Julie von Haefen (D-Wake) on Tuesday renewed her long-running push to fund it in the legislature, as dozens of public school advocates rallied outside the North Carolina General Assembly.
This marks the seventh time von Haefen has filed the proposal, which has repeatedly failed to receive a committee hearing. “I’m tired of asking. I’m tired of filing these bills. I’m tired of standing at microphones begging this state to fund public education.”
It also comes on the heels of an April 2 state Supreme Court decision that shifted the responsibility of funding the Leandro plan back to the General Assembly. Von Haefen’s bill requires the state to fund the series of reforms laid out in the Leandro case, a decades-long school funding lawsuit first filed in 1994.
At the same time, some two dozen advocates gathered outside the North Carolina General Assembly on the opening day of the short session to press for action on both the Leandro plan and broader education funding priorities. Speakers described schools strained by staffing shortages, limited student services and growing disparities between districts.
Xavier Adams, a teacher at Orange High School and the 2022 North Carolina beginning teacher of the year, said schools are increasingly relying on temporary funding streams to maintain programs while struggling to keep educators in the profession.
“Teachers should not and cannot continuously rely on a patchwork of nonrenewable grants,” he said.
Morgan Taylor, a student advocate from Pitt County, said her district has lost nearly 70 teaching positions, leading to larger class sizes and fewer extracurricular programs. “It means bigger classes, less support and teachers who are doing everything they can, but are stretched,” Taylor said.
“Fully funding public schools should not be a debate. It should be a given,” Taylor said.
Other speakers pointed to gaps in mental health services and special education staffing, saying families are absorbing more of the burden as school resources fall short.
Stein pitches NC budget with teacher raises, tax cuts, Medicaid funding

On the same day, Gov. Josh Stein proposed a new budget that includes about $2.3 billion for public education. The plan calls for an average 11% raise for teachers and would raise starting teacher pay to the highest level in the Southeast.
North Carolina ranks second to last in the nation in per-pupil spending and below all neighboring states in starting teacher pay.
“If we’re going to continue to build our economic success, there’s one area where we cannot afford to fall behind: our public schools,” said Stein. “Our children are our future, and investing in them and the educators that help them learn will pay off for generations to come.”
The North Carolina Association of Educators released a statement praising the budget proposal. “It raises teacher pay at all levels, restores master’s pay, eliminates the mid-career pay plateau, invests more in Exceptional Children programs, and ensures every child can eat breakfast at school,” said Tamika Walker Kelly, NCAE president.
